cover.title: IT Operating Model
cover.subtitle: Capability Model, Current State Analysis & IT Cost Savings Case
cover.hook: Culligan's IT operating model is not a model. It is 24 separate IT operations running in parallel, each replicating the same capabilities independently. The cost of that duplication is measurable. The path to reducing it is clear.

kpis.label: Est. total IT cost incl. people

cover.source: Source: Culligan Spend Cube June 2026 · March 2026 P&L. People costs excluded from spend cube.

rows.finding: Culligan's IT estate is the unmanaged residue of 20+ acquisitions. Every business unit runs its own IT operation independently — its own ERP, CRM, service desk, managed service contracts, and IT staff — with no group mandate to standardise, consolidate, or govern. Culligan operates one business model across three regions, but runs its IT 24 separate ways.

19 of 19 operating BUs buy software independently ($34.8M) · 19 separate MSP/IT service contracts ($15.7M) · 10 different ERP instances across the group · 19 separate CRM instances, despite a $7.2M group Salesforce EA sitting unused · 15 separate cloud tenancies with no group FinOps · 15+ separate service desks costing an estimated $45–80 per ticket vs. $12–20 at best-in-class · Group CIO in place but mandate limited to Corporate enterprise agreements — no authority over BU technology decisions · Estimated $80–130M in IT headcount cost entirely invisible in the spend cube · EMEA pays $5M more in IT Spend than Americas at equivalent revenue scale, directly attributable to running six national IT operations independently.

rows.dimension: Impact on the Culligan operating model
rows.finding: IT fragmentation directly undermines the Culligan operating model in four ways: (1) Scale benefits are destroyed — a $3.8B enterprise negotiates 19 separate software contracts instead of one, paying small-company rates across every BU. (2) Operational visibility is broken — no group IT performance data, no consolidated SLA reporting, no single view of the technology estate. (3) Integration is structurally blocked — 10 ERP instances and 19 CRM instances make group-level data consolidation, cross-BU reporting, and post-acquisition integration progressively harder and more expensive. (4) Risk compounds silently — security patching, access management, and change control are managed independently per BU with no group oversight, creating a patchwork risk posture that no single person can see.

$22–44M in annual run-rate savings at Year 3, comprising $12–22M from H4 IT operating model changes (service delivery consolidation, headcount rationalisation, MSP renegotiation, demand governance) and $12–23M from H2 Infrastructure, H3 application rationalisation, and H5 vendor agreements — all of which are unlocked by H4 governance. Conservative estimates using lower-bound Gartner, Forrester, IDC, and Info-Tech benchmarks.

Extend Group CIO mandate to cover all BU-level IT decisions. Establish an IT architecture board with cross-BU authority. Introduce an IT chargeback model to create a financial incentive for BU compliance. Commission the PwC TBM baseline to make the $80–130M headcount cost visible. Without these steps, no consolidation programme — application, infrastructure, or vendor — can be executed at group level.

Wave 1 (0–6 months): Extend Group CIO mandate, establish IT architecture board, complete SaaS and telecom vendor audit — $4–10M quick wins. Wave 2 (6–18 months): Deploy group ITSM (ServiceNow), migrate first BU service desks, launch Salesforce consolidation — $6–14M. Wave 3 (18–36 months): Full service desk consolidation, IFS ERP roll-out, cloud FinOps, IT chargeback — $12–20M additional.

capabilityModel.hero: Culligan operates one business model across three regions — but runs it 24 different ways. And IT is paying for every duplicate.
capabilityModel.section1: Culligan operates across 59 legal entities, 24 business units, and three regions — delivering water softening, filtration, dispensing, and purification to residential, commercial, and industrial customers across more than 100 countries. The business capability model maps what Culligan needs to be able to do — independent of how it does it, who does it, or which systems it uses — across all 24 BUs simultaneously. It is the analytical foundation for the PwC IT operating model hypothesis.

capabilityModel.section1a: Culligan's portfolio was assembled through more than 20 acquisitions over the past decade. Quench, ZIP Water, Harvey Water Softeners, ZeroWater, and Paragon Water Systems were all built independently before becoming Culligan entities. The result is three structurally distinct operating archetypes:

archetypes.bus: ZIP ANZ, ZIP UK, Harvey, Culligan AUS

capabilityModel.callout: No two BUs were designed to operate together. The technology fragmentation visible in the capability map — 10 separate ERPs, 19 CRM instances, 14 FSM tools — is not an architectural choice. It is the unmanaged residue of 20+ acquisitions where integration was never prioritised. The capability model provides the first common framework across all 24 BUs that makes the total cost of that fragmentation visible.

capabilityModel.coreInsight: Every domain row shows the same capability names across all three region columns. "Route planning and optimisation" appears in Americas, EMEA, and APAC. "Financial management and reporting" appears in all three. The capabilities are identical across a $1.87B, 24-BU, 100-country enterprise. What differs is the technology estate that supports them — and that is where the savings are.

currentState.title: IT operating model — current state
currentState.lead: Culligan's IT operating model was never designed. It is the residue of 20+ acquisitions, each of which left behind its own IT organisation, its own vendor contracts, its own service desk, and its own governance structures. Every BU manages IT independently — from provisioning laptops to managing ERP licences to running a helpdesk.
currentState.doingWellTitle: What Culligan is already doing well

doingWell.observation: Corporate has negotiated a $7.2M Salesforce enterprise agreement — the largest single IT spend item in the group. The commercial leverage is already secured.
doingWell.impact: The EA unit economics make BU migration financially attractive. Migrating BUs eliminate their standalone CRM contracts while paying into an EA already funded at group level. Net cost impact is neutral-to-positive from the first BU consolidated.

doingWell.observation: Corporate funds a $1.7M group security operations centre (Crowdstrike or equivalent), providing centralised threat monitoring across the estate.
doingWell.impact: Avoids 24 BUs independently procuring endpoint security. Equivalent per-BU coverage purchased independently would cost an estimated $3–4M group-wide — a $1.3–2.3M annual saving already being realised.

doingWell.observation: Culligan has selected IFS as the group ERP standard and built a deployment template, establishing a clear architectural direction for the 10-instance consolidation.
doingWell.impact: Template investment is sunk. Every BU migrated onto IFS eliminates a standalone ERP instance — licence, support, and integration costs. The savings case strengthens with each migration.

doingWell.observation: A Group CIO exists at Corporate level, providing the senior IT leadership role from which cross-BU mandate and architecture governance can be extended.
doingWell.impact: Extending the Group CIO's mandate is a governance decision, not a hiring process. The cost and lead time of establishing group IT leadership is already absorbed.

doingWell.observation: Workday has been selected as the group HR system and is partially deployed, establishing a precedent for group platform adoption across BUs.
doingWell.impact: Demonstrates BU-level migration to a group platform is operationally feasible. The Workday deployment is the proof of concept for IFS ERP and Salesforce CRM consolidation.

mustAct.area: Group CIO mandate has no cross-BU reach
mustAct.observation: The Group CIO's authority is limited to Corporate enterprise agreements. BUs select, procure, and manage technology independently with no reference to group standards.
mustAct.impact: Every consolidation opportunity — ERP, CRM, service desk, cloud, vendor agreements — requires BU-by-BU negotiation. Without mandate, fragmentation grows with every acquisition and every BU technology renewal cycle. This is the single most costly governance gap.

mustAct.area: 15+ separate service desks, no ITSM standard
mustAct.observation: Every BU operates its own service desk — some internal, some outsourced to local MSPs. No group ITSM platform, no SLA framework, no consolidated performance data.
mustAct.impact: Est. $45–80 per ticket vs. $12–20 at best-in-class. The excess cost of fragmented service delivery is $2.4–4.7M annually on IT Spend alone, before accounting for the productivity cost of inconsistent service quality.

mustAct.observation: No group architecture function. Each BU selects technology independently. 19 CRM instances, 10 ERP instances, and 14+ FSM tools — all three numbers are growing.
mustAct.impact: Each new point solution added at BU level increases the eventual consolidation cost and timeline. Without an architecture board to enforce standards, the fragmentation premium compounds annually.

mustAct.area: No group change or release management
mustAct.observation: ERP patches, CRM updates, and infrastructure changes are managed entirely within BU boundaries. A vulnerability patched in one BU may remain unpatched in others for months.
mustAct.impact: Uncoordinated patching creates a material security risk exposure. A single breach in an under-patched BU carries remediation costs that would dwarf the investment in group change governance.

mustAct.area: IT budgeting invisible at group level
mustAct.observation: IT budgets are set at BU level with no group consolidation. The $69M IT Spend represents an estimated 30–40% of true IT cost. The $80–130M headcount cost is entirely unmanaged at group level.
mustAct.impact: Without a group IT cost baseline, Culligan cannot identify duplicate spend, benchmark against peers, or build a credible business case for consolidation investment.

mustAct.observation: EMEA spends $19M in IT Spend against a comparable revenue base to Americas at $14M. The $5M premium is the direct cost of six national IT functions operating independently.
mustAct.impact: $5M annually in excess IT Spend attributable solely to EMEA fragmentation — before headcount. EMEA is the highest-priority region for IT operating model consolidation.

currentState.fragmentationTitle: IT fragmentation by capability — the numbers

fragmentation.observation: Every BU buys software independently. No group master agreements below Corporate level.
Every BU has its own MSP or internal IT team. Germany alone: $2.9M to a local MSP.
Separate telecom contracts per BU. No group mobile or fixed-line framework.
15 BUs have separate cloud tenancies (AWS/Azure). No group FinOps. No consolidated cloud org.
10 BUs on separate ERP instances (SAP, Navision, local). IFS is group template but not yet deployed.
19 BUs on separate CRM. Corporate holds $7.2M Salesforce EA that BUs are not consolidated onto.

currentState.headcountLead: The IT Spend of $69M is estimated to represent only 30–40% of true IT cost. Applying Gartner's benchmark that people represent 60–70% of IT cost in comparable industrial services organisations, total IT cost including headcount is approximately $150–200M annually. This means $80–130M of IT cost sits entirely outside the current spend data.
currentState.headcountCallout: The fragmentation multiplier A consolidated IT operating model at Culligan's scale ($3.8B enterprise) would require approximately 150–250 group IT FTEs. The current fragmented model implies roughly 1–2 IT staff per BU managing local IT, plus local MSP relationships — potentially 50–100 people performing duplicated functions that a shared model would consolidate into 20–30 roles. That is the invisible savings pool.

Applied to Culligan's profile: industrial services / FSM company, $3.8B revenue, multi-BU, post-acquisition context.

benchmarking.industryTitle: Industry evidence for shared services consolidation
industryEvidence: Gartner — IT operating model maturity (2024) Gartner's Strategic Roadmap for the Service-Optimising IT Operating Model places Culligan at the "decentralised" archetype — the starting point of a five-stage maturity scale. Moving to a shared services model is associated with 15–25% reduction in IT run costs through headcount right-sizing, licence pooling, and process standardisation. Gartner's critical finding: organisations that attempt tool consolidation without governance first achieve only 30–40% of available savings. Extending the Group CIO's mandate across all BUs is the critical prerequisite.

Forrester — Total Economic Impact of IT consolidation (2025–2026) Forrester TEI studies consistently show 295–480% ROI over three years for organisations consolidating fragmented multi-system environments. Forrester's 2026 ERP consolidation study found 100%+ ROI with a 16-month payback for mid-market organisations consolidating multiple ERP instances — directly analogous to Culligan's 10-instance situation.

IDC — Global Business Services (2024) IDC identifies IT service desk as the highest-return shared services consolidation target — ahead of finance and HR — because it is the most standardisable function. IDC's single-point-of-service model delivers continuously optimised workloads and SLA-driven accountability. The managed services market is growing at 13.6% CAGR to 2030 — Culligan's fragmented MSP spend will cost progressively more if not consolidated.

Info-Tech Research Group — service desk consolidation blueprint (2024) Info-Tech quantifies the tool consolidation saving alone — licensing, administration, training, integration — at 20–35% of current ITSM tooling spend, before labour efficiency gains. Critical finding: consolidation requires executive sponsorship to maintain legitimacy. Organisations without a mandate from the top fail to complete consolidation because BUs resist.

savings.totalAddressable: Total addressable saving — H3 + H4 + H5 combined (excl. H1 and H2 which are quantified separately)
savings.h4Title: IT service & support — the H4 anchor opportunity
h4Lead: This is the clearest and most immediately actionable opportunity. 19 BUs each paying for IT services independently, $15.7M group-wide. Germany alone pays $2.9M to a local MSP. Nordics $1.4M. Iberia $1.1M. All delivering the same capability at different rates with no group leverage.

The mechanism is straightforward: replace 15+ separate service desk arrangements with a single group L1/L2 shared service on a common ITSM platform (ServiceNow is the leading candidate). A virtual consolidated service desk operating across time zones achieves the same structural benefit as a single location.
savings.h4Sizing: Sizing basis $15.7M IT services invoices × 15–30% benchmark saving = $2.4–4.7M invoice saving. Gartner's maturity research: moving from decentralised to shared services is associated with 15–25% reduction in IT run costs including headcount. Applied to Culligan's estimated 24–48 local IT FTEs, this implies an additional $3–6M people saving not visible in the spend cube.
savings.h4Dependency: Critical dependency This change cannot be driven from Corporate IT without executive mandate. The H4 workstream must begin with a governance recommendation — formalising the Group CIO's cross-BU mandate and establishing the IT architecture board — before a technology recommendation. Without executive authority, every service desk migration will be vetoed by a local general manager citing business disruption.

itLeadershipStructure.title: IT Accountability
itLeadershipStructure.lead: Wave 1 requires a decision on how IT accountability is distributed before governance can be formalised. The table below maps each IT function to who owns it today and who would own it under each option — the key question is not what title regional leaders hold, but which functions sit centrally versus regionally under each model.

decisionCriteria.title: Decision criteria — Group CIO vs BU ownership
decisionCriteria.lead: Six criteria determine whether an IT function sits centrally under the Group CIO or is retained at business unit level. A function that meets the majority of the left-hand conditions below belongs centrally. A function that meets the right-hand conditions is a candidate for BU retention — with governance conditions applied.
columns: Group CIO owns it centrally when…

rows.bu: Spend is BU-specific, below group aggregation threshold. Includes niche local tools, local regulatory subscriptions.

rows.groupCio: Function touches data/processes flowing between BUs (reporting, intercompany, customer data, post-acquisition integration).

rows.groupCio: Consistency creates value (one SLA, one security posture, one ITSM workflow, etc.).

rows.bu: Function creates genuine competitive differentiation (connected product technology, localised customer experience tools).

structuralPrinciple.title: The structural principle that cannot move
structuralPrinciple.body: Whichever option Culligan chooses, the Group CIO must own group IT shared services — the service desk, ITSM platform, ERP template, cloud organisation, and enterprise agreements — as a single budget, not fragmented into regional IT operations. The moment a regional CIO or CTO owns their own service desk and infrastructure budget, the savings case is materially undermined. Regional IT leaders must be consumers of group platforms, not operators of regional IT stacks. The IT architecture board and chargeback model enforce this boundary.

roadmap.title: Recommended sequence — three waves
roadmap.lead: The savings opportunities are interdependent. The recommended sequence maximises early wins while building the governance foundation required for the larger structural changes. Nothing in Waves 2 or 3 is achievable without the governance investment in Wave 1.

waves.actions: Formalise Group CIO cross-BU mandate. Establish IT architecture board. Commission TBM baseline (PwC H4). Complete SaaS and telecom vendor audit (H5 quick wins). Renegotiate top 5 MSP contracts as a group.

Select and deploy group ITSM platform (ServiceNow). Migrate first 5 BU service desks. Standardise L1/L2 triage processes. Launch corporate Salesforce roll-out to first 3 BUs. Begin IFS ERP pilot (2 BUs).

Complete service desk consolidation (all BUs on group model). Accelerate IFS ERP roll-out. Consolidate cloud tenancies under group FinOps. Design and implement group IT chargeback model. Full headcount right-sizing.
waves.saving: $12–20M additional. H3 + H2 + H4 headcount savings.

roadmap.governanceLead: None of the above savings are achievable without first establishing the governance structures that make consolidation possible. Three investments are non-negotiable:

governance.does: The Group CIO exists but currently manages Corporate enterprise agreements only. The mandate must be extended to cover all BU-level technology decisions — platform standards, architecture, vendor contracts.
governance.without: The Group CIO has no authority to enforce group standards at BU level. Every consolidation initiative requires BU-by-BU negotiation.

governance.does: Quarterly governance body (Group CIO chair, BU IT leads) to ratify technology decisions and manage the application consolidation roadmap.
governance.without: No mechanism to enforce the IFS ERP template, Salesforce consolidation, or ITSM standardisation.

governance.does: BUs on group platforms pay the consolidated rate; BUs operating outside group standards pay the full undiscounted cost. Gives the Group CIO commercial leverage.
governance.without: No financial incentive for BUs to move to group platforms. Fragmentation continues to grow.
